title: Gandhari curses Krishna
hook: a grieving mother turns to Krishna and curses him, and he answers with something close to a smile
carry: sthitaprajna: steady, even when the curse comes
tomorrow: what secret does Kunti tell at the river?

segments.voice: Yesterday in Stri, Gandhari was given sight and turned it on the women searching the field. Your line was the equal eye, their grief as your own.

She has been talking to Krishna the whole time. Look at this widow, look at that mother, look at my son. And somewhere in that long walk across the field, the grief turns. Gandhari stops describing and starts accusing. You could have stopped this, she tells him. You had the power. You had the words. Both sides listened to you, and you let it happen. The curse in this book's title isn't aimed at the Pandavas. It's aimed at Krishna, standing right beside her.
screen: `THE GRIEF TURNS.` → `"YOU COULD HAVE STOPPED THIS."` → `THE CURSE IS FOR KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Gandhari reaches for the power her discipline has given her, the power she held back with Yudhishthira. Because you stood by while the Kurus and the Pandavas destroyed each other, she says, your own kinsmen, the Vrishnis, will kill one another. You yourself will die alone, in a wild place, by an inglorious means. And the women of your house will weep over their dead, the way the women of mine are weeping now. Krishna doesn't argue or defend the war. In Ganguli's telling he answers calmly, almost with a smile. I already knew this, he says, in effect. My people can be destroyed by no one but themselves. Then he gently turns her grief back to her. The war came, he says, from your son's choices, and from your own failure to restrain him. Get up. Don't give yourself to sorrow. Gandhari falls silent. So the curse lands, and Krishna accepts it. The book doesn't settle whether she was right to blame him. But many teachers see Krishna here living what he taught Arjuna on this same field: the sthitaprajna, the one of steady wisdom, whose mind isn't shaken in sorrow, who is free of craving, fear and anger. And Hindu devotion makes room for Gandhari too. A grieving mother says something almost unsayable to Krishna, whom the epic honors as God, and he takes it without striking back. Today, when someone's grief comes at you as blame, steady isn't cold.
screen: `SHE CURSES KRISHNA'S PEOPLE` · `HE ANSWERS CALMLY` · `"I ALREADY KNEW"` · then, large: `STHITAPRAJNA: STEADY WISDOM`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees and bring to mind a question you've wanted to shout at life, or at God, or at whoever was in charge when something went wrong. Breathe in and let it be as loud as it really is; breathe out and notice that it can be said and the world still holds. If you pray, you can bring that question to God just as it is, the way Gandhari brought hers to Krishna. If you don't, let it be heard by the quiet.
Stri. Woman. The book where a mother's grief becomes a curse on Krishna, and he stays steady.
Your line: sthitaprajna, steady even when the curse comes. Tomorrow, the water offered for the dead, and a secret. That's day eight hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Gandhari's curse on Krishna is told in temple discourses, plays and retellings of the epic, storytellers link it to the later end of Krishna's own clan, and teachers point to his calm answer as the Gita's steady wisdom.

fork.reveal: Krishna answers calmly, says he already knew, and gently tells her to rise from her grief: steady, the way the Gita's sthitaprajna is steady.

original.note: curse: a word spoken with the power of a person's discipline, which in the epics comes true.

chat.meaning: Cursed by a grieving mother, Krishna answered calmly and didn't strike back: the Gita's sthitaprajna, steady in sorrow, free of anger.
